lesson.title: Rebase a feature branch onto main and resolve conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

sources.title: Rebase a feature branch onto main and resolve conflicts

steps.title: Set up repo and diverged branches
steps.instructions: In the empty workdir run `git init -b main`, commit app.txt, then `git switch -c feature/login` and make three commits (1st and 3rd editing the same line of app.txt, 2nd adding a new file). Switch back to main, make two commits editing that same line, then run `git log --oneline --graph --all` to see the fork.

precision_checks.label: Branches have diverged
precision_checks.command: test $(git rev-list --count main..feature/login) -ge 3 && test $(git rev-list --count feature/login..main) -ge 2

targets.caption: History forks: feature and main have diverged

explanations.topic: Goal: bring main's commits into the feature branch without a merge commit
What git rebase main does: sets commits aside and replays them on main's tip
Why it's called rebasing: old base commit vs new base commit
Fast-forward merge and linear history

hints: Start in an empty folder and run `git init -b main`, then commit an app.txt containing a single line.
Run `git switch -c feature/login`. Make three commits: the 1st and 3rd change that same line of app.txt, and the 2nd adds a new file.
Run `git switch main` and make two commits that change that same line of app.txt to different text.
Check the shape with `git log --oneline --graph --all`. You should see a fork with 3 commits on feature and 2 on main.
common_mistakes: Making the main commits before creating the feature branch, so the branches never diverge.
Editing different lines on main and feature, so the later rebase produces no conflict.
Forgetting `git add` before committing, which leaves the changes uncommitted.
Using an older git where `git init -b` isn't supported, which leaves the default branch named master.

steps.title: Check the branch isn't pushed
steps.instructions: Switch to your feature branch (`git switch feature/login`) and run `git branch -a`. Confirm it has no remotes/ counterpart, so it is safe to rebase.

explanations.topic: Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed
Rebasing changes commit hashes, so local and remote no longer match
Pulled copies diverge and teammates can lose work; merge doesn't rewrite history
Use git branch -a to see whether the feature branch exists on the remote

hints: Before rewriting history, find out whether this branch already exists on a remote.
git can list local and remote-tracking branches together with one flag on `git branch`.
Run `git branch -a`. Remote branches show up as `remotes/origin/...`.
If your feature branch appears under remotes/, don't rebase it. If it only appears locally, it's safe to continue.
common_mistakes: Running plain `git branch`, which shows only local branches and hides remote ones.
Running the command outside the repository folder, which gives 'fatal: not a git repository'.
Seeing `remotes/origin/main` and thinking the feature branch was pushed. Only a remote entry for the feature branch itself matters.
Not running `git fetch` in a repo with a real remote, so the remote branch list is out of date.

steps.title: Start rebase and hit conflict
steps.instructions: On feature/login run `git rebase main`, then `git status`. Confirm git reports a rebase in progress with app.txt as both modified.

targets.caption: Rebase pauses on the first conflicting commit

explanations.topic: Rebase reapplies feature commits one by one, so each may conflict
Feature branch commits originate from an older main commit; rebasing moves the base
A conflict pauses the rebase; git status shows which commit and how many remain
Resolving rebase conflicts works like merge conflicts

hints: Make sure you're on your feature branch (git branch) before running git rebase main.
After the rebase stops with a CONFLICT message, run git status to see the rebase state.
Look for 'rebase in progress' and the 'Unmerged paths' / 'both modified' section in the status output.
If no conflict appears, your branches may not edit the same lines; revisit step 1's setup.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase main while on main instead of the feature branch.
Running git rebase feature/login from main, reversing the direction.
Panicking at the conflict and running git rebase --abort before inspecting status.
Main and feature not editing the same lines in app.txt, so no conflict occurs.
Typing 'git rebase origin/main' with an outdated remote instead of the local main.

steps.title: Resolve conflict and stage file
steps.instructions: Open app.txt, delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers keeping the correct line, then run `git add app.txt` and `git status`.

targets.caption: Conflict markers Git inserted. Delete them and keep the right lines.

explanations.topic: Remove conflict markers and keep the correct code
Run git add for every conflicted file
Rebase uses --continue instead of commit, unlike merge

hints: Open app.txt in your editor and look for the lines Git added around the conflicting section.
Delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines, keeping only the content that should remain after the rebase.
Save the file, then run `git add app.txt`. Do not commit yet.
Run `git status`. app.txt should appear under 'Changes to be committed' with no 'both modified' entries.
common_mistakes: Leaving a stray ======= or >>>>>>> line in the file
Keeping both versions verbatim when only one is correct
Forgetting to save the file before running git add
Running git commit instead of staging and moving on to git rebase --continue
Running git add before the file is actually fixed

steps.title: Continue rebase past commit two
steps.instructions: Run `git rebase --continue` (save the message with Esc then `:wq`); fix the next conflict in app.txt, `git add app.txt`, and `git rebase --continue` again. Finish with `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph`.

targets.caption: Continue the rebase instead of committing
Git stops again on the third commit's conflict
Back on your branch, not mid-rebase

explanations.topic: Git opens vim to edit the commit message; Esc then :wq saves and quits
Changing git's default editor
Non-conflicting commits are applied automatically; rebase pauses at the next conflict
Third commit conflicts again, so the rebase pauses once more
No commits left, so continuing concludes the rebase
Use git status to confirm you're no longer in a rebasing state

hints: After staging the resolved file, don't commit. Tell the rebase to carry on with its own continue command.
Run `git rebase --continue`. If a terminal editor opens, that's just the commit message.
In vim, press Esc, type `:wq`, then press Enter to save and close.
Git should apply the second commit by itself and then stop with a CONFLICT on the third commit. That conflict is the expected result.
Open app.txt and resolve the conflict the same way you did for the first one.
Delete every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> line, then save the file.
Run git add app.txt, then git rebase --continue. When the editor opens, type :wq and press Enter.
Run git status. It should say 'On branch …' with no 'rebase in progress' message.
common_mistakes: Running `git commit` instead of `git rebase --continue`.
Getting stuck in vim, for example typing :wq without pressing Esc first or forgetting Enter.
Running --continue before `git add` on the resolved file, which leaves conflicts unmerged.
Thinking the new CONFLICT means something went wrong. It is the third commit's expected conflict.
Quitting vim with `:q!`, which aborts the commit message.
Leaving conflict markers (<<<<<<< / >>>>>>>) in app.txt before staging it
Running git rebase --continue before running git add on the resolved file
Getting stuck in the vim commit-message editor instead of typing :wq
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue
Leaving the rebase half-finished, so git status still reports 'interactive rebase in progress'
